passage:
In the inter-school camp dining hall, a parent volunteer stopped Noor at the long table. 'Beta, you sit at that side table. These children are from pure-veg families.' Noor was holding the same dal and rice as everyone else. Noor's face burned.
Akash, who had been saving the seat, stood up. 'She's eating exactly what we're eating.'
'Rules are rules,' the volunteer said. Noor went to the side table anyway, head down.
Akash went straight to Mrs. Pillai, the camp teacher. Within ten minutes she was in the hall. She told the volunteer clearly, 'Nobody at this camp eats apart because of their religion. That is exclusion, and it stops now.' Then she carried her own plate to the side table, sat beside Noor, and asked Akash to bring the others over.

qa.q: Who did Akash go to for help?
qa.a: Mrs. Pillai, the camp teacher.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when told to sit at the side table?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and hurt, her face burning, made to feel less than the others even though her plate was the same.

qa.q: What did Mrs. Pillai do that others could learn from?
qa.a: She came the same day, named the separate seating as exclusion, stopped it, and sat with Noor herself so Noor was not alone.

qa.q: How might the parent volunteer see things after Mrs. Pillai's words?
qa.a: The volunteer may feel embarrassed or defensive at first, but has been told clearly that separating a child by religion is wrong.

grounding: Shows a teenager told to eat apart because of religion, the hurt it causes, and an adult who names the exclusion as wrong and ends it.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal Bhaiya,
Something happened that I can't stop thinking about. Nisha's family had a lunch after their griha pravesh, and our whole class group was invited except me. Nisha told me quietly that her Dadi had said 'our kind only' in the kitchen. I laughed like it didn't matter. Then I cried in the bus.
That evening I told Papa. He put down his tea and said, 'Rashmi, this is caste, and it is wrong. It is not about you.' He called Nisha's mother that same night, calmly. She was shocked; she hadn't known about the list. Today Nisha came to school with sweets from the puja and said her mother is talking to her Dadi. I don't know if I'll go next time. But I felt heard.
Rashmi

qa.q: What did Nisha's Dadi say in the kitchen?
qa.a: 'Our kind only.'

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling after hearing why the invitation never came?
qa.a: Rashmi felt deeply hurt and humiliated, laughing it off in front of Nisha but crying in the bus.

qa.q: What did Papa do right when Rashmi told him?
qa.a: He named it as caste and wrong, told Rashmi it was not about Rashmi, and called Nisha's mother calmly that same night.

qa.q: How might Nisha feel about what her Dadi did?
qa.a: Nisha seems uncomfortable and sorry, which is why Nisha told Rashmi quietly and later brought sweets.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager left out of a meal because of caste, the deep hurt it brings, and adults who name the exclusion as wrong and act to end it.

passage:
On the second night of the school camp at the forest department hostel, the cook set Vijay's plate on a separate bench by the kitchen door. "You sit here," he muttered, and said something about Vijay's surname.

Vijay, fifteen, sat. His ears burned. Through the doorway he could see the others laughing at the long table. His friend Suraj half-stood, then looked around for a teacher.

Mr D'Souza, the camp in-charge, had seen. He walked over, picked up Vijay's plate, and carried it to the long table himself. "Everyone eats together here. Vijay, sit by me."

Then he went into the kitchen. Nobody heard all of it, but they heard, "This is wrong, and it stops tonight. I'm calling the warden and your supervisor now."

Vijay ate slowly, hands still shaking. Suraj pushed his extra papad onto Vijay's plate without a word.

qa.q: Where did the cook set Vijay's plate?
qa.a: The cook set Vijay's plate on a separate bench by the kitchen door.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling as he sat on the separate bench?
qa.a: Vijay felt humiliated and hurt, ears burning, watching the others laugh together at the long table.

qa.q: What did Mr D'Souza do that was right?
qa.a: He named the exclusion as wrong, brought Vijay to the shared table, and called the warden and the cook's supervisor that same night.

qa.q: What was it like for Suraj to watch it happen?
qa.a: Suraj was upset and unsure what to do alone, looking for a teacher, and then quietly showed support with his papad.

grounding: Shows a teenager made to eat separately because of his background, the hurt it causes, and an adult naming it wrong and acting at once.

passage:
Dear Tsering,

Something happened at our class potluck today, and I need to tell someone who'll get it.

One of the parents organising it put a sign on a table in the corridor: "Non-veg tiffins here." So Aslam, two others and I ate outside while everyone else was in the classroom. I had brought Amala's momos. I felt like the food was dirty, and so was I.

Then Rukmini ma'am came out. She looked at the sign for a second, took it down, and said, "Nobody eats in a corridor in my class. That isn't a food rule, that's leaving people out, and it's wrong." She carried our tiffins inside, put separate serving spoons on every dish, and made a veg side and a non-veg side on the same long table.

After the bell I saw her talking to that parent, calmly, for a long time.

Two girls asked for my momo recipe.

Pema

qa.q: What did the sign in the corridor say?
qa.a: The sign said "Non-veg tiffins here."

qa.q: How did Pema feel eating in the corridor?
qa.a: Pema felt ashamed and hurt, as if both the food and Pema were dirty.

qa.q: Which of Rukmini ma'am's actions ended the exclusion?
qa.a: She took the sign down, called it wrong, brought everyone to one table with separate spoons and sides, and spoke to the parent that same day.

qa.q: How might the organising parent see the teacher's talk?
qa.a: The parent may feel embarrassed or defensive, perhaps having thought the sign was just practical, without seeing how it made children feel less.

grounding: Shows a teenager sent to eat apart because of diet, the hurt of it, and a teacher naming the exclusion as wrong and ending it that day.

passage:
Promise you won't make it a big thing? Okay. I'm Mahima, I've lived next door to Uma my whole life, and until this year I went to every puja at her house.

This time Uma's Dadi was visiting from the village. When I came to the door, she stopped me. "Your people eat outside," she said, and pointed to the steps. I didn't even understand at first. Then I did.

I went home and sat in the bathroom so Mummy wouldn't see my face.

An hour later Uma's mother knocked on our door. She'd heard from Uma. She said to Mummy and me, "What happened was wrong. It won't happen in my home again. I've told Mummyji so." Then she asked me to come back and eat with them, at the table, next to Uma.

I went. Dadi didn't speak to me. But Uma held my hand under the table the whole time.

qa.q: Where did Uma's Dadi point when Mahima came?
qa.a: She pointed to the steps.

qa.q: What did Mahima feel after being turned away at the door?
qa.a: Mahima felt deeply hurt and humiliated, hiding in the bathroom so Mummy wouldn't see.

qa.q: What did Uma's mother do that made a difference?
qa.a: Within the hour she came over, said plainly that it was wrong and wouldn't happen again, told Dadi so, and brought Mahima back to eat at the table.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt holding Mahima's hand under the table?
qa.a: Uma likely felt sorry and protective, wanting Mahima to know she was on her side.

grounding: Shows a teenager excluded from a neighbour's meal because of who her family is, the deep hurt, and an adult naming it wrong and acting the same day.

passage:
Saturday: At Rohit's birthday lunch, Rohit's grandmother handed Yash, fifteen, a steel plate and pointed him to the steps outside. Everyone else sat on the mats inside. "It's our custom," she said, not looking at him. Nobody said anything. Yash ate two bites, said he felt sick and walked home. He didn't tell his parents. He felt like dirt.
Monday: In class Yash didn't speak at all. At break, Aparna ma'am, the class teacher, asked him to help carry books and gently asked what was wrong. It came out in a rush. She put the books down. "Yash, what happened was wrong, and it is not your fault. You are not less than anyone." That afternoon she called Yash's parents and then Rohit's mother, and she reported it to the principal.
Wednesday: Rohit came to Yash's desk, red-faced. "Mummy says it was wrong. I'm sorry I didn't say anything." At lunch he sat beside Yash and they shared a tiffin.

qa.q: Where was Yash told to eat at Rohit's birthday lunch?
qa.a: On the steps outside, with a steel plate.

qa.q: How did Yash feel after being sent to eat on the steps?
qa.a: He felt deeply hurt and humiliated, like dirt, so ashamed he didn't even tell his parents.

qa.q: What did Aparna ma'am do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She named the exclusion as wrong, told Yash it was not his fault, and that same day called both families and reported it to the principal, acting to end it.

qa.q: How might Rohit have felt when he apologised?
qa.a: Rohit seemed ashamed and sorry, red-faced about staying silent, and wanting to show Yash he was on his side.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager made to eat separately because of caste custom, who feels less than others, and an adult who names the exclusion as wrong and acts.
